title: Take nothing (Luke 9:1–17)
hookLine: the twelve sent out light, then five thousand fed

cards: The charger, the spare charger, the snacks, the just-in-case jacket, the bag that won't close. That's packing for a weekend.
Now take a mission instead: go to towns you've never seen, heal the sick, preach the kingdom of God. The packing list comes back mostly crossed out. That's chapter nine of Luke.
The twelve are sent out on their own, and when they come back, there's a hungry crowd of thousands and almost no food.

teach.h: NO STAFF, NO BAG, NO BREAD, NO MONEY.
teach.b: Jesus gives the twelve power over devils and diseases, and then the list: "Take nothing for your journey; neither staff, nor scrip, nor bread, nor money; neither have two coats."
A scrip is a traveler's bag, the kind you'd carry food in. Stay in whatever house takes you in. If a town won't receive you, shake the dust off your feet and move on.
Why so little? Luke doesn't say. One way to read it: traveling light means depending on others.

teach.h: TRAVELING LIGHT MAKES ROOM FOR WELCOME.
teach.b: The twelve have to knock on doors and be received; their poverty makes room for someone else's welcome. And it works: they go through the towns preaching and healing everywhere.
When they come back, Jesus takes them aside to a desert place near Bethsaida, and the crowds follow. Evening comes. The twelve suggest the practical thing: send them away to find food and lodging.
Jesus answers: "Give you them to eat." They count what they have: five loaves and two fishes, and about five thousand men. Here Luke slows down.
Jesus takes the bread, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, and gives to the disciples to set before the crowd.
Took, blessed, broke, gave. Catholics hear nearly the same movements at every Mass, in the words of the Last Supper.
Everyone eats and is filled, and twelve baskets of fragments are gathered up, from what the twelve had called too little. First they learn to go out with nothing.
Then they learn that what little they have, placed in his hands, is enough to feed a crowd.

how: Catholics hear the feeding of the five thousand from Luke on the solemnity of the Body and Blood of Christ in the year of Luke's Gospel, and some religious orders vowed to poverty take the mission of the twelve as part of their pattern of life.

o: pack only what you can carry yourself
travel light, and depend on others' welcome
refuse any gift offered on the road

games.q: sent out, then fed — tap the pairs.
p: a town that won't receive you
shake the dust off your feet

s: Jesus told the twelve to pack carefully for their mission
he said take nothing: no staff, bag, bread, money or spare coat.
Jesus suggested sending the crowd away to find food
the twelve suggested it. Jesus said give you them to eat.
the feeding uses nearly the same gestures as the Last Supper
took, blessed, broke, gave; at the Supper Luke says gave thanks. Catholics hear these movements at every Mass.

games.q: you're one of the twelve. it's evening, five thousand people are hungry, and you have five loaves and two fish. what do you suggest?
o: send them away to buy food in the villages.
share out the bread to whoever's closest.
ask the crowd to go home.
games.why: the twelve say send them away. Jesus says give you them to eat, blesses what they have, and twelve baskets are left over.

practice: Picture what you're carrying into today, and not just in your bag: the grudge, the five worries, the backup plan for the backup plan.
Pick one thing you can set down, and imagine placing it on a table and walking out the door without it. If you pray, place it in God's hands, like the five loaves.

wordCard.voice: Take nothing. Jesus' packing list for the twelve: no staff, no bag, no bread, no money, so they'd depend on welcome, and then learn that a little is enough. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing for the journey. Room, then, for someone else's welcome. Day four hundred fifty-eight, done.
